newsitem.title: USA: Fed holds interest rates steady, but for how long?.
newsitem.headline: Fed holds interest rates steady, but for how long?.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
The U.S. Federal Reserve decided on Tuesday to leave interest rates unchanged in hopes that the economy will slow from its recent break-neck pace.
But many analysts said it is only a matter of time before the central bank will need to raise rates further to prevent the economy from overheating and keep inflation in check.
"It ain't over til it's over," said Nicholas Perna, chief economist at Rhode Island-based bankers Fleet Financial Group. "The (economic) numbers are going to dictate the Fed's actions."

Wall Street stock and bond prices bounded higher in the wake of the Fed's decision. The Dow Jones industrial average of blue-chip shares rose 74.58 points to a near-record 7,303.46. The key 30-year Treasury bond gained 7/32 point, or $2.19 per $1,000 face value.
Lawmakers, businessmen and labor unions also cheered the Fed's move, saying that it was good news for the economy.
Higher rates tend to slow the economy and dampen inflation by making it more expensive for everyone from consumers to corporations to borrow money.

"From living rooms to boardrooms, anyone concerned with economic growth and continued high unemployment can breathe easier," Jerry Jasinowski, President of the National Association of Manufacturers, said. "The Fed recognized that there is no need to fix an unbroken economy."

The economy grew at a 5.6 percent annualized clip in the first quarter, its fastest pace in more than nine years. But inflation has remained quiescent, with consumer prices rising at a year-on-year rate of 2.5 percent in April.
Analysts said that the combination of political pressure and expectations of slower growth was enough to convince the Fed not to follow up its March rate increase with another now.

At its March 25 meeting, the Fed tightened credit for the first time in more than two years, bumping up short-term rates by a quarter percentage point, in part because of a perception that the economy was growing too fast for its own good.

In a speech in New York earlier this month, Greenspan defended the March increase as a prudent step to insure against the threat of higher inflation but acknowledged that the move had generated an unusual amount of criticism.
"They're sensitive to the political pressure," Gary Thayer, senior economist at St. Louis-based brokers A.G Edwards and Sons, said.
Greenspan also forecast in that speech that economic growth would moderate and that inflation would stay stable in the coming months.

That is what seems to be happening. Retail stores saw their sales slump in April while production at the nation's factories was flat. Economists said that growth in the second quarter is widely expected to be about half that of the first.

But there are doubts about how long that combination of moderate growth and tepid inflation will last, economists said. Jobs are plentiful and consumers are confident, pointing to the possibility of a pick-up in growth later this year.
At 4.9 percent, the unemployment rate stands at its lowest point in nearly 24 years and is at a level that in the past has led to stepped-up wage demands and higher inflation.
That is why many analysts expect the Fed to eventually raise rates further, perhaps as early as its next policy-making meeting on July 1-2.

"My thought is that we are going to find the economy resuming much more rapid growth in the third quarter, and that eventually the Fed will have to raise rates significantly," former Fed Gov. Lyle Gramley said.
In his speech at New York University earlier this month, Greenspan said the central bank needed to be wary.
"While there is scant evidence of any imminent resurgence of inflation at the moment, there also appears to be little slack in our capacity to produce," he said.
"Should the expected slowing in the growth of demand fail to materialize, we would need to address any emerging pressures in product and credit markets," Greenspan added.

The federal funds rate, the rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans, currently stands at 5.50 percent. The discount rate that the Fed charges the banks for money is 5.0 percent.
